summary.text: De Moivre's formula connects complex numbers and trigonometry, using the expression cos x + i sin x, sometimes abbreviated cis x.
Expanding one side and comparing real and imaginary parts gives expressions for cos nx and sin nx in terms of cos x and sin x.
As written it is not valid for non-integer powers, but generalizations of it give explicit expressions for the nth roots of unity.

facts.label: Named after
facts.value: Abraham de Moivre, who never stated it in his works

facts.label: Valid powers
facts.value: Whole-number powers, even when x is a complex number

facts.label: Proof method
facts.value: Mathematical induction covers the natural numbers

facts.label: Chebyshev link
facts.value: The cos nx formula is a Chebyshev polynomial of cos x

items.prompt: The formula carries de Moivre's name. Which statement about that naming is accurate?

options.label: He proved it first in a famous 1748 book
It is named after him although he never stated it in his works
It is named for whoever first proved it by induction
He named it after Euler, who discovered it

items.explain: The formula is named after Abraham de Moivre, although he never stated it in his works.

items.prompt: A student raises the expression cos x + i sin x to a power of one half and applies the formula directly. What goes wrong?

options.label: Nothing; the formula works for every power
It only works for even powers
The formula is not valid for non-integer powers
It requires x to be measured in degrees

items.explain: The formula does not hold for non-integer powers n, and the derivation relies on an integer power.

items.prompt: A complex number is raised to a power that is not a whole number. What is true of the result?

options.label: It is always a single real number
It always equals the whole-number result
It is undefined
It can take several different values

items.explain: If a complex number is raised to a non-integer power, the result is multiple-valued.

items.prompt: Generalizations of the formula give explicit expressions for the complex numbers z such that zⁿ = 1. What are those numbers called?

options.label: Roots of unity
Conjugate pairs
Chebyshev polynomials
Unit vectors

items.explain: The nth roots of unity are the complex numbers z such that zⁿ = 1, and the generalizations can express them explicitly.

items.prompt: Mathematicians expand one side of the formula and compare real and imaginary parts, assuming x is real. What does this produce?

options.label: A proof that the formula fails for whole numbers
Expressions for cos nx and sin nx
A way to find the roots of unity
A rule for turning radians into degrees

items.explain: Comparing the real and imaginary parts gives useful expressions for cos nx and sin nx in terms of cos x and sin x.

items.prompt: To prove the formula for every natural number, the argument shows it holds at the start and that if it holds for one number it holds for the next. What technique is that?

options.label: Mathematical induction
Proof by contradiction
Checking a finite list of cases
Drawing a picture on the unit circle

items.explain: Showing that one case implies the next, together with a base case, proves the result for all natural numbers by the principle of mathematical induction.
